cultivar: Seed-grown zairai bushes and ordinary summer leaf
processing: Mature leaves are steamed or boiled, piled in a warm room for a few weeks so moulds ferment the heap, then dried; the finished dark tea (Toyama kurocha) is boiled, poured into a bowl with a pinch of salt and whisked to a froth with a double-headed bamboo whisk.
harvest_season: Summer and early-autumn leaf from the current year; the tea is made in autumn and drunk through the year.
appearance_dry: Coarse, dark brown to black leaf pieces and stems, dry and crumbly, smelling faintly of hay and cellar.
appearance_liquor: Reddish-brown and clear before whisking, then topped with a dense pale foam.
taste_profile: Mild, earthy and slightly musty with a savoury, soft body and a faint sweetness; the salt-and-foam serve makes it taste almost like a light broth.

brewing.notes: Simmer the leaf in a kettle for ten minutes or so, pour into a wide bowl, add a pinch of salt and whisk briskly with the paired 'meoto' chasen until it foams; drink foam and liquid together. The leaf can be topped up with water and simmered again.

vintage_note: Made from the current year's summer leaf by a very small number of producers around Asahi town and sold locally and by a few specialist shops in bags with the production year; it is a dried fermented tea that keeps a year or more and is not aged on purpose. Buy it with the double whisk if you want the real ritual.
description:
Batabatacha is a fermented tea from Asahi on the Toyama coast, drunk in a way found nowhere else in Japan: boiled, poured into a bowl with a pinch of salt and whisked into a thick foam with a double-headed bamboo whisk, which makes the 'bata-bata' sound that gives it its name. The tea itself is a mould-fermented dark tea, locally called Toyama kurocha or Birudani batabatacha after the hamlet that makes it, and the whisking is traditionally a social ritual, tied to Buddhist memorial days and neighbourhood gatherings.

Mature leaves are steamed or boiled, piled in a warm room and left for a few weeks while moulds ferment the heap, then dried; there is no lactic stage, which puts it closer in spirit to Chinese dark teas than to the sour banchas of Shikoku. The finished leaf is coarse, dark and crumbly and smells of hay and cellar. Mature leaf and fermentation leave it very low in caffeine.

To drink it the local way, simmer about 10 g in a litre of water for ten minutes, pour into a wide bowl, add a pinch of salt and whisk briskly with the paired 'meoto' chasen until the surface is covered in dense pale foam; drink foam and liquor together. The flavour is mild, earthy and slightly musty with a savoury, broth-like body, and the salt turns it into something closer to a light soup than a tea. The leaf can be topped up with water and simmered again. Steeped like sencha in a kyusu it is thin and dull, which is why the ritual matters.

It is made from the current year's summer leaf by a very small number of producers and sold locally, at a few Toyama shops and by specialist dealers in bags with the year; the double whisk is sold alongside it and is worth buying if you want the real thing. It keeps a year or more as a dried fermented tea, and there is no ageing market or grade.

If the salt-and-foam idea appeals, Okinawa's bukubuku-cha is the other whisked-foam tea to look for; if the fermentation does, goishicha and awabancha are the next stops.
